items.prompt: What does a flat "no" hide?
choices: The reasoning behind the refusal
The size of the favor requested
Who first made the request
items.explanation: The requester hears the conclusion but cannot tell whether it is a real limit.

items.prompt: What does a silent "yes" hide?
choices: The reason the request was made
The cost someone will absorb later
The name of the person asking
items.explanation: Saying yes without mentioning the cost does not remove it; it moves the cost to later.

items.prompt: Which answer feels smooth now but causes trouble later?
choices: Saying no and giving a reason
Offering two options to choose from
Saying yes without mentioning the cost
items.explanation: A silent yes pleases the requester in the moment and leaves the bill for later.

items.prompt: A flat "no" leaves the requester unable to tell what?
choices: Someone who never agreed to the cost
The person who asked, right at the start
Nobody, because the cost just goes away
items.explanation: With no reasoning visible, a real constraint and plain unwillingness look the same.

items.prompt: Who ends up paying for a silent "yes"?
choices: The person who asked, up front
Someone who never agreed to the cost
Nobody, because the cost disappears
items.explanation: The cost is real; it lands later on whoever has to absorb it, often the person who said yes.

items.prompt: Maya says "sure" to helping Sam move on Saturday, and she has already promised to help her sister paint that day. What is the likely result?
choices: Both happen smoothly with no trouble at all
Sam and her sister both turn down her help
One of the two promises gets broken or rushed
items.explanation: Two commitments cannot both fit the same hours; something gives, and nobody chose what.

items.prompt: True or false: a silent yes removes the cost of the request.

items.explanation: Costs do not disappear when unspoken. They surface later, unplanned.

items.prompt: What flaw do the flat no and the silent yes share?
choices: Both of them take far too long to say aloud
The real trade-off stays hidden from the requester
Both of them need a third person to be involved
items.explanation: Neither answer shows the requester what is actually being traded, so they cannot weigh it.

items.prompt: Which reply is a silent overcommitment?

"Sorry, I can't make it this Saturday, but thanks for thinking of me."
"Saturday has my sister's painting; could another day work for you?"
items.explanation: The first reply accepts without surfacing any of the competing commitments. The second and fourth name a constraint and an alternative; the third is a plain refusal.

Naming the constraint, offering options, and letting the requester choose

items.prompt: Which phrase is trade-off pushback?

"I'm just too busy right now, so I'm afraid it's not going to work out."
"Sure, I'll make it work somehow; don't worry about it, I'll sort it out."
items.explanation: It names a concrete cost and offers a choice. The others hide the trade-off.

items.prompt: Why is the decision handed back to the requester?
choices: It saves the responder some time and effort overall
They know which trade is acceptable from their side
It lets the responder avoid ever having to say no
items.explanation: Only the requester knows whether a date is firm or flexible.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT part of trade-off pushback?

A polite way of delivering only a refusal

A third option beyond yes or no

A vague promise to try and see how it goes
A concrete option the requester can pick

items.prompt: Which reply is true trade-off pushback?

"Saturday is impossible for me this time, so please ask somebody else instead."
"I can come Saturday afternoon if I leave the painting early, or Sunday morning; which helps more?"
"Whatever you decide is completely fine with me, I'll go along with it all."

A polite excuse that nobody is expected to check

A feeling, not a checkable fact
A concrete offer with options to choose from

choices: So the responder is able to win the argument
So the reply sounds more formal and official
So the requester can judge and negotiate it
items.explanation: A checkable constraint can be weighed. An uncheckable one can only be believed or doubted.

"Saturday is kind of hectic for me, to be honest"

The requester cannot tell what to trade against

Only the word "busy", said with feeling

No: studying is never a real constraint at all

items.learnMore:
Facts, not mood

A constraint is useful when the requester can check it and decide what to trade against it. Naming specific commitments and their dates does this; naming a feeling does not.

items.reflection: Next time you feel "too busy", try listing exactly what is committed and when. Did the list change how you wanted to answer?

items.prompt: What is step 1?
choices: Offer the options to the requester
Check what is already promised and by when
Say no and give a short reason
items.explanation: You cannot name a true constraint before you know your real load.

items.prompt: In step 2 you name the constraint using...
choices: Mood, not facts
An apology
Facts, not mood
items.explanation: Facts are what the requester can evaluate.

items.prompt: In step 3 you offer...
choices: Real options to choose between
One take-it-or-leave-it answer
Nothing yet
items.explanation: Choices are what turn a refusal into a negotiation.

items.prompt: Step 4, with a peer, is to...
choices: Decide silently on their behalf
Ask the requester for the priority call
Withdraw the offer without saying why
items.explanation: The requester owns the priority and makes the choice.

items.prompt: Why verify the load first?
choices: So you can refuse faster
So the requester sees your calendar
So the constraint you name is true
items.explanation: A constraint that turns out false costs you trust.

items.prompt: Which order is correct?
choices: Verify, name, offer, hand back
Offer, verify, apologize, name
Hand back, name, verify, offer
items.explanation: Each step builds on the one before it.

items.prompt: "Two tasks are due Friday" is the output of which step?
choices: Verifying the load
Naming the constraint
Offering options
items.explanation: It states the checked load as a fact.

items.prompt: With a large power gap, step 4 becomes...
choices: Ask permission before you are allowed to say no
Skip the step because the requester outranks you
Flag the trade-off and state your default plan
items.explanation: You still surface the trade-off, but as information plus a plan.

items.prompt: Someone says "I think I'm booked," without checking, and later finds the afternoon was free. Which step failed?
choices: Offering too many options for the requester to compare at once
Verifying the real load before naming a constraint
Handing back the final decision to the requester before explaining
Stating facts about the week rather than describing how it feels
items.explanation: A constraint that was never verified can turn out to be false.
items.reference:
The four-step structure
1 verify the real load
2 name the constraint with facts
3 offer real options
4 hand the call back, or flag it and state your plan
Why: each step removes a guess: whether the constraint is true, specific, actionable, and owned by the right person.
items.learnMore:
Four steps before you speak

Check what is actually promised, say it with facts, give the requester real choices, and then either ask for a priority call or, with a large power gap, flag the trade-off and state your default plan.

Common mistake

Skipping the check and naming a constraint from memory or mood.

items.reference:
Four kinds of trade
time: ships later
scope: delivers less
priority: something else moves
person: someone else takes it
Why: naming the kind of trade you can offer turns "I'm busy" into a menu the requester can pick from.
items.learnMore:
A menu of trades

Almost every option you offer changes one of four things: when it is done, how much is done, what else gets pushed, or who does it.

Common mistake

Offering a trade you cannot actually make, such as moving a deadline you do not control.
items.reflection: Think of a request you accepted last month. Which of the four trades could you have offered, and which one would the requester have picked?

items.prompt: Sam asks Maya to help move on Saturday. Which set of three options spans different kinds of trade?

Saturday morning, Saturday afternoon, or Saturday evening of the same weekend
Maybe Saturday, maybe not; I'll text you on that morning to say which

items.prompt: Omar must review two contracts by Thursday for Lena, but a hiring panel and the quarterly report fill his week. Which reply matches the pushback version?

Compare the actual words

Holding the request fixed and changing only the reply shows exactly which elements carry the difference: a concrete constraint, concrete options, and a decision handed back.

Believing that mentioning any constraint at all is enough.

items.prompt: The CEO's chief of staff asks for a deck by tomorrow, which would mean skipping an incident review. Which reply fits best?
choices: "Which do you want me to prioritize here, the deck for tomorrow or the incident review?"
"Taking the deck means the incident review moves to Thursday; I'm planning that unless you tell me otherwise."

"Sure, whatever you need from me, I'll make sure that it gets done by tomorrow."
items.explanation: It names the trade-off and states a plan, leaving room to redirect.
items.reference:
When the requester outranks you
peer: "Which matters more?"
much more senior: "I want to flag this before I confirm"
same facts, different delivery
Why: with a big power gap, an open question can read as pushing a decision upward; a flagged trade-off plus a plan does not.

Same information, different delivery

The constraint and the trade-off stay named in both cases. What changes is whether you pose it as a question or give it as information with a stated plan.

items.prompt: Omar checks and finds a free afternoon. Which reply is best?

items.reference:
When there is nothing to trade
checked load shows slack: say so plainly
never invent a constraint to seem careful
"no trade-off" is still a visible answer
Why: the method surfaces the real trade-off, including none; it depends on the constraint being true.
items.learnMore:
Surface what is real

If the load check shows room, saying so plainly is the honest answer. Making up a constraint to look appropriately busy erodes the trust the method is meant to protect.

Treating pushback as something to do on every request.
